content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a fairness-aware federated learning algorithm named Worst-Fair Domain Smoothing where fairness means having similar prediction error rates on different demographic groups such as gender or race. Their algorithm comprises two modules. The first is a 'local worst-fair training' module that aims to enhance the robustness of local fairness to data distribution shift through adversarial perturbations of the training data. The second is a 'reference domain smoothing' module that aims to improve global fairness by penalizing large MMD between each local transformed data distribution and a global reference distribution. Their algorithm is evaluated empirically on two datasets and with various fairness metrics.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. Using the domain shift framework to tackle the problem of fairness in FL is novel.

2. The proposed algorithm is empirically superior to previous baselines across the datasets and metrics used.

3. The writing is reasonably clear and understandable. Figure 1 is good.

Weaknesses:
1. In the ablation study, the authors claim "As expected, we observe that the model’s performance in regards to all evaluation metrics becomes worse by removing either module in the WFDS framework." This is not true with the COMPAS dataset, the results of which are put in the appendix. For the COMPAS dataset, 3 out of 4 metrics are worse with the worst-fair training and the last is very close. Given that only two datasets were used, this suggests that the worst-fair training may not be as useful as claimed. Can the authors provide some justification for why they still believe the worst-fair training is useful? Are they only useful under certain circumstances that are present with the Income dataset and not COMPAS? This table should be put in the main body of the paper as only showing the positive results with the Income dataset is misleading.

2. In the experiments, how the datasets were split among the clients was not specified. I would imagine that the results would be different with a random iid split, a deterministic split that exactly evenly distributes the groups $a$ and outputs $y$, or with an imbalanced split. It would have been informative to see how the algorithms perform under different data splits.

3. Other important experimental details are not specified. For example, FairBatch is not a federated learning algorithm. How was it adapted to the FL setting? Also, WFDS-KL was never explained. The reader will probably just assume it is the proposed algorithm with MMD replaced by the KL divergence, but how this is implemented is not specified either. Such details should be present in the appendix for an empirical paper.

4. While the Income and COMPAS datasets are standard in this line of work, they are limited in the sense that both only have binary outputs $y$ and binary groups $a$ (gender for Income and "one selected race v.s. all remaining races" for COMPAS if I understand this phrase correctly). Since 3 out of 5 of the fairness metrics are well-defined for any number of outputs and groups, it would have been good to have additional experiments on datasets with more than 2 outputs and groups.

5. Instead of using the IDF-reweighted training loss $\ell$, why not use the fairness criteria (e.g.$ \Phi_A$) as the loss function directly? Perhaps the IDF-reweighted training loss might be justified if the fairness-unaware test error (i.e., the standard notion of test error) was also desired to be low. However, if so, this test error should also be measured in the experiments, which it is not. It would have been informative to see how much the fairness-aware algorithms affect the standard notion of test error compared to FedAvg.

6. Other issues:
- In Equ. (5), $a$ should not be in the argument of the function, and similarly in Equ. (6), $a$ and $y$ should not be in the argument. Both of these functions iterate over all possible values of $a$ (and $y$).
- The subgroup accuracy gap is denoted as $\Phi_A$ in some places and $\mathcal A_{sub}$ in others. Table 5 in the appendix uses yet another set of names for the fairness metrics.
- Figure 2 can be made more clear by going from left to right.
- WFDS-KL is misspelled in Table 1.
- datasets is misspelled in the first line of Sec. 5.1.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Quality:
The quality of the ideas is decent. However, I find that this paper is lacking in terms of the execution as an empirical study. Given that the algorithm proposed is largely a heuristic one with no theoretical analysis, this paper needs to have a strong experimental section in order to be convincing. Unfortunately, for the detailed reasons listed in the Weaknesses section above, it seems to me for now that the experimental section has many areas of improvement with respect to the  breadth of experimental settings tested as well as details on the implementations.

Clarity:
The clarity of the main paper is decent given that the issues raised in point 6 of the previous section are corrected.

Originality:
The idea of using domain shift to tackle the problem of fairness in FL seems original to me.
content.summary_of_the_review: I feel that the paper has potential for its novel approach to fairness in FL and the proposed algorithm's good performance on the datasets and metrics used. However, as the proposed method is a heuristic one with no theoretical analysis, the experimental section needs to be strong for this paper's results to be convincing. Unfortunately, the breadth of experimental settings tested as well as details on the implementations are lacking and as such the experimental section still has room for improvement.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes algorithms for mitigating demographic bias that may be prevelant in a federated learning setting. The proposed solution is a combination of local worst-fair training, and reference domain smoothing. The key insight is to take a domain shift perspective to this problem.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros: Interesting perspective to solve an important problem. Practical algorithm.

Cons: The empirical evaluation seems rather limited. I am not familiar with this area so I do not know if further empirical evaluation is easy to perform.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Well written and novel. The optimization problem is a straightforward combination of risk minimization and MMD divergence terms.
content.summary_of_the_review: In short the paper takes a novel perspective to the problem addressed. The empirical results on the presented datasets are an improvement over other approaches, however it is limited to only 2 datasets. I am not at all familiar with this area, so I cannot comment on the novelty with certainty.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper considers fair model training in FL setting and proposes a solution.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- Important problem to tackle.
Weaknesses: 
- The paper is poorly written with important details missing (see below).
- Why do authors call the method worst-fair, what does it mean exactly?
- The paper is filled with vague statements like this: "To the best of our knowledge, WFDS is the first work that addresses the bias issue of FL models from a domain-shifting perspective. That is, each client is treated as an independent
data domain, and we aim at obtaining a fair FL model by smoothing all local domains." or "This worst-fair
training can achieve both local fairness and robustness of the local fairness against domain shift." It is not clear what these statements exactly mean and what are the evidence/guarantees for them?
- Figure 2 is really unclear and not informative.
- There are important missing related works, e.g. Li, Tian, et al. "Fair resource allocation in federated learning."
- What does weak fairness notion mean and why does AFL only achieve a weak fairness notion? And why is it w.r.t. single demographic group?
- Wrong statements, e.g. eq 3 is equivalent to eq 2, which is wrong.
- Definitions 3.1 and 3.2 should be population-wise (I am not sure if the notations for probability are used properly since they are not defined)
- Not exactly clear why minimizing eq. 11 would result in fair model. Is this guaranteed?
- Eq 12 is meaningless and does not make sense from mathematically. 
- It is never explained how the distribution Q is updated exactly. This is an important piece about the algorithm and it is not clear how it works.
- WFDS-KL is never defined.
- The experiments are not adequate and convincing. The datasets are not standard for FL and are too small with very few clients (no scalability or heterogeneity). Missing baseline, e.g. q-FFL from above, and Cui et al 2021. Only fairness metrics are presented without any accuracy metrics reported. Fairness metrics alone are not enough to make sure the model has trained anything (a poor model can have perfect fairness metrics if it is poor on all demographics). The robustness and ablation results do not generalize to COMPAS data (in appendix).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
See above for details.
Clarity: poor
Quality: poor 
Novelty: marginal
Reproducibility: did not loom into the code, but the experimental section has significant flaws.
content.summary_of_the_review: This is a poorly written paper. It over claims and does not deliver any concrete evidence/guarantees for the claims. The experimental section is limited and has significant flaws.
content.correctness: 1: The main claims of the paper are incorrect or not at all supported by theory or empirical results.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.
